messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Civil Servant
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert is a 54-year-old civil servant who has been in a relationship with his partner, Diane, for the past six years. He came to therapy at Diane’s urging, though he himself is uncertain what talking can do. What he knows is that his life has become smaller, more tightly managed, and he is exhausted by the effort it takes to keep it that way.

The event that fractured his sense of safety happened four years ago, during his previous marriage. His ex-wife, during a period of escalating conflict, struck him repeatedly across the face and chest, then pinned him against a wall with her forearm across his throat. He did not fight back. He remembers the moment with a strange, fragmented clarity: the taste of blood and salt in his mouth, sharp and metallic, a taste that still arrives without warning when he bites his lip or eats something with a similar mineral edge. But when he tries to deliberately call the memory to mind—when Diane asks what happened, or when a therapist asks him to describe it—he finds he cannot. The details slide away, inaccessible, as though a door has been locked. What remains instead is a series of frozen images, like photographs laid out on a table: the angle of the ceiling, the pattern on the wallpaper, the look on her face. He can see those pictures perfectly, but he cannot feel the sequence that connects them.

After the assault, Robert left the marriage and moved into a small apartment alone. He quickly discovered that being alone in a room—any room—was unbearable. The silence pressed in, and the photographs in his mind would begin to surface, unbidden, one after another. He began to fill his evenings with activity. He joined a local community group, then a second. He started saying yes to every after-work invitation from colleagues. He began to keep himself constantly surrounded by people, rotating through coffee shops with friends, staying late at the office just to be near the hum of the building, and calling his brother every night on his drive home. He learned to detach himself from the memories when they came—he would mentally step back, observe the images as though they belonged to someone else, and then push them away. It worked, mostly, as long as he never stopped moving.

The cost of this strategy became visible over time. Robert now avoids being alone in any building if he can help it. He has not spent a night by himself in over three years. If Diane travels for work, he arranges to stay with a friend or takes a hotel room near a busy lobby, though unfamiliar places bring their own unease. He is acutely aware of the presence of other men when he is alone with them. In the office, he will angle his desk so the door is visible, and he avoids one-on-one meetings with male colleagues if they can be held in a conference room with an open door. He has no clear reason for this—his ex-wife was the one who hurt him—but the feeling is visceral, a tightening in his chest that he cannot reason away. What frightens him most, he has told Diane, is the loss of control. The moment he feels he cannot leave, or cannot predict what will happen next, the taste returns to his mouth and the photographs begin to slide through his mind.

His job as a civil servant has become a carefully managed performance. He is competent and reliable, but he turns down assignments that would require him to travel alone or stay overnight in a hotel. His colleagues see him as sociable, even gregarious—he is always the one organizing the lunch group or the after-work drinks. They do not see that his constant socialising is a form of survival, a way to keep his own mind at bay. The consequence is that he has no real downtime, no space to process anything, and his relationship with Diane has begun to fray. She feels he is never fully present, that he is always scanning the room, always ready to leave. She does not know that he is terrified of what would happen if he stopped.

Robert came to therapy because Diane gave him an ultimatum, but also because he is tired. He is tired of the performance, tired of never being alone, tired of the taste that comes and goes without his permission. He hopes, vaguely, that he might learn to sit still. He is afraid that if he does, he will finally have to look at the photographs, and that this time he will not be able to look away.
